findings: B [Ensemblens invändning mot textremsan är ett svepskäl som döljer ett annat motstånd.] — killed by Ett svepskäl är det inte and by Så lyder ensemblens invändning, och jag skriver under på den: she signs up to the ensemble's objection instead of dismissing it.

justification: Key A: Från och med nästa spelår bör texten gå på varje föreställning på stora scenen, inte på fyra utvalda is the demand, and Kostnaden är verklig och ska räknas med plus Ändå ska den bäras is the explicit concession that the acting is bound harder to the script and that this cost is real and to be borne.

findings: A [Den är märkt med slingans symbol.] — killed by Slingans symbol finns längst ned på varje uppslag i programbladet: the loop symbol sits at the foot of every spread, not on the captioned-performance row.

B [Den upprepas längst ned på varje uppslag.] — killed by the same span: it is the symbol, not the row, that repeats on every spread; the row is a single line, en egen rad, inklämd mellan syntolkning och skolföreställningar.

C [Den anger vem som sköter tekniken.] — killed by Längre bak i programbladet står Ingegerd Hörnfeldt under rubriken Text och teknik: the named technician appears further back in the programme, under a separate heading.
justification: Key D restates the opening sentence: de textade föreställningarna en egen rad, inklämd mellan syntolkning och skolföreställningar.

findings: B [Hovarna klarade sig med broddar.] — killed by mot det hjälper varken broddar eller lättare lass.

findings: A [Hushållen turades om och delade på vändorna.] — killed by Var gård körde för sig, och sällan väntade någon in grannen.

C [Barnen fick lasta medan de vuxna var ute och körde.] — killed by Barnen provar den med hälen som vi gjorde, utan att det ska bli någon färd: the children in the text belong to the present day and make no journey at all.

D [Man fortsatte tills sista lasset var hemma.] — killed by Ett lass som inte är hemma vid tio blir liggande till nästa natt: work stopped when the crust went, and a load not home by ten simply lay until the next night.
justification: Key B: Veckorna kom när de kom and Man såg på himlen och bestämde sig kvällen innan — the days could not be fixed ahead, only read off the sky the evening before; some winters gave four mornings and some gave none.

findings: A [He drove the cone through to the bottom of the bed at each point.] — killed by how many blows take it to a hundred millimetres read against The floor is 130 millimetres of washed silica sand: the count stops at 100 mm in a 130 mm bed.

B [The weight was let fall by hand, from whatever height each point seemed to need.] — killed by under a ring weight raised to a collar and let fall: the drop height is fixed by the collar, which is what makes the two grids comparable.

D [The spread between one arena and the next is wider than the spread between his two visits.] — killed by The gap between my February morning and my July afternoon is still wider than the gap between this school and any other school I test., which states the reverse.
justification: Key C: in the cold the first blow took the cone two-thirds as deep, and the count nearly doubled — two-thirds as deep is a shallower first blow, and a nearly doubled count is a higher count, so both figures point the same way.

findings: A [The wax had worn off the grains in the lower part of the bed.] — killed by the wax he brought up from the bottom was in better condition than the wax at the top.
B [The sand had broken down into finer grains than the specification called for.] — killed by the grains he sieved came out much as the original specification had them.

C [Below the tines the bed had stayed loose, out of reach of the hoofprints above it.] — killed by Eighty millimetres of it had not been turned since the day it was laid, and under nine years of hoofprints it had gone firm enough to lean a spade on.
justification: Key D is the cored result: In the top 50 millimetres the fibre came out at about 8 per cent by weight; lower down it was nearer 3.. Arithmetic reconciles: 3 per cent against 8 per cent is well under half, and tines set to 50 mm in a 130 mm bed explain the split, since Harrowing lifts fibre, and fibre keeps sand from packing.

findings: A [They went down more recently, so their sand has not had nine years of hooves on it.] — killed by some of them older than this one and by The waxed ones move, whatever their age.: age is explicitly ruled out as the variable.

C [A membrane under them holds the water in, so the bed does not dry through the day.] — killed by laid over a membrane and crushed stone: the only membrane in the text lies under this waxed school, which is precisely the type that does move, and no water-retaining function is attributed to it anywhere.

D [They are read at a different hour, so the change falls between his two grids.] — killed by He has the same pair of grids from a hundred and forty other arenas and by the morning grid and the afternoon grid sit almost on top of one another: the same pair of grids, morning and afternoon, is what is compared across every arena.
justification: Key B: In the schools laid on plain sand and fibre and kept damp with a sprinkler, the morning grid and the afternoon grid sit almost on top of one another. sets the unwaxed, watered schools against The waxed ones move, whatever their age., and the mechanism paragraph supplies the cause — The wax is a paraffin blend, and it is doing most of that work, stiff below about six degrees and slack above about twenty-five. The stem asks what is suggested, which licenses that causal step.

findings: B [She reads what the yard has since done as an answer to the soundness question.] — killed by The tester measures a surface; there is no horse above the cone.: the tine change and the unordered heaters address the bed and the temperature, not soundness, which the text deliberately leaves open.

C [She treats the riders’ account as the thing the readings were brought in to correct.] — killed by For two winters the riders here have been saying that the school changes under them read against Both figures moved, and they moved together: the readings confirm the riders; what they correct is the yard's blaming of the machine, the mix and the man.

D [She rates the trade’s brochures the fuller answer to the question the yard is asking.] — killed by That is a good deal less than the trade’s brochures offer, and it is worth more than they are.: the brochures offer more but are judged worth less.
justification: Key A: Here Pallenmoor is careful, and the care is the most useful thing about him. — the writer's one explicit valuation is of the limits he puts on his own figures.

findings: A [In the cold the grains are probably freezing to one another in a school with no heating.] — killed by Below about six degrees the coating is stiff, the grains lock together: the stiffening agent is the paraffin coating, not ice, and the cold readings were taken above freezing (with the school at three degrees).

B [A school that is kept warm will ride in February much as it rides in July.] — killed by Above about twenty-five it goes slack, the grains slide past one another, and the floor gets deep: warmth does not remove the hot end of the range, and no heated school is ever tested — Heaters have been costed and not ordered.
D [The tractor’s work may matter more to the school than the temperature does.] — killed by The temperature is doing more in that room than the tractor is.
justification: Key C names both causes the text establishes: the wax's response to room temperature, and The leveller’s tines were set to 50 millimetres. against The bed is 130., the mismatch that sorted the bed into a loose layer riding on a hard one. The text ranks temperature above the tractor but keeps both in play, which is exactly what C claims.

findings: A [Hence] — killed by again there has been no signal: the unanimous ending is a second instance of the same unexplained coordination, not a consequence of the unanimous start.
B [Rather] — killed by the same span: nothing in the clause corrects or replaces what precedes it, so a corrective adverb has nothing to correct.
D [Elsewhere] — killed by two hundred people find the same half-second: the ending happens in the same hall, so a contrast of place is empty.
justification: Key C: 'Equally' marks the parallel second case — the start is unanimous, and equally the ending is: five seconds later the sound stops.

findings: B [cut] — killed by for the length of one clap you are alone with an opinion nobody asked for: 'cut in' means to interrupt, but the fear is that nobody else will add their applause.
C [fall] — killed by the same span: 'fall in' means to get into line or formation, the wrong relation for a room adding applause.

D [break] — killed by the same span plus That is why the second pair of hands matters more than the first: 'break in' is to interrupt or intrude, whereas the text's own gloss is a second pair of hands adding itself to the first.
justification: Key A: 'join in' is the collocation the sentence requires — the risk is that the room may not join in.

findings: A [transaction] — killed by about how long is decent, conducted at speed and without words: a transaction is an exchange of goods or money and cannot be 'about how long is decent'.
C [bargain] — killed by the same span: a bargain names the deal struck, not the wordless process the sentence says is being conducted.
D [settlement] — killed by the same span: a settlement is the outcome, while the coming-down is a  presents the coming-down itself as the process.
justification: Key B: 'negotiation' is the only option that names a process, and it takes both 'about how long is decent' and 'conducted at speed and without words'.

findings: A [rehearsed] — killed by No one has agreed to anything, there is no conductor to watch: nothing about the hall's response is prepared, and the word yields no concession against the length limit.
B [outspoken] — killed by the same requirement: applause is not speech, and the word gives the 'Although' nothing to concede against it is not permitted to run long.

C [brief] — killed by Although what a hall gives an eight-year-old is : 'Although ... is brief, it is not permitted to run long' runs the concession twice in the same direction, so the clause collapses.
justification: Key D: 'wholehearted' supplies the contrast the 'Although' needs — warm in kind but still capped in length: Four or five seconds, then a ragged tail.

findings: A [narrowly] — killed by A room asked for a big hand for a stranger will give one : no margin or scale is in play, only the quality of the sound.
C [instinctively] — killed by the same span: the hand is asked for, i.e. prompted, which is the opposite of instinctive; the unprompted case is the one the recorder player got.
D [eagerly] — killed by everybody present can hear that it is not the same sound the recorder player got: the point of the sentence is that this hand is audibly lesser.
justification: Key B: 'dutifully' names the obliged, perfunctory clap that the second half of the sentence then contrasts with the genuine one.

findings: B [A spoilt sample can be spotted by its colour before it leaves the ward.] — killed by Nothing shows on the ward; the colour comes with the spinning..
C [Samples for blood gases go by tube because they cannot be left waiting.] — killed by Blood gases have never gone by tube; a porter walks those down..

D [The number of rejected samples fell once the loop was slowed down.] — killed by The loop runs at the speed it always has.: the fall of about half followed the foam lining of two bins, not any change of speed — Two bins are lined with foam, and rejects are down by about half.
justification: Key A is her own attributed finding: It’s the stop at the far end that does it,, set against Between stations the shocks were tiny..

findings: A [Ruddiforth’s neighbour answered the claim without bringing the railway company’s plan into the letters.] — killed by The neighbour’s attorney enclosed a tracing of the railway company’s deposited plan..

B [The quarrel began because the thorn on the bank had been left untended.] — killed by cut from above by one and cleaned from below by the other and by both sides agree the thorn was last laid in 1839: the hedge was worked by both farms, both sides agree on its last laying, and it had never been in dispute before 1845.

C [The surveyor came to the bank after the attorneys had begun to write.] — killed by The previous October a surveyor had chained and pegged the line along the bank read against In November 1845 Ephraim Ruddiforth’s attorney claimed: the pegging was the October before the November claim, so it preceded the letters.
justification: Key D: the claim covers the bank, the ditch and the timber from the stone gap down to the lane, and the pegged line runs from the ash to the culvert, which is the same stretch once An ash grew in the stone gap; a culvert ran under the lane. is applied — the ash marks the stone gap, the culvert marks the lane. The timeline reconciles: peg October 1845, claim November 1845, letters to March, scheme abandoned autumn 1846, both farms laying the thorn together in 1851.
